rashi:a2.1: It is sold for the needs of a burnt offering, and its payment is non-sacred: since he did not consecrate the animal itself.
rashi:a2.2: Except for the payment for the limb: that he may not receive its payment. Since inherent sanctity has come upon it, he is not permitted to sell it, and if he sold it, it is not sold, since it is his burnt offering; and since it does not go out to non-sacred status, as it is unblemished, sanctity does not take effect on the money for the limb. Therefore it is not sold. And if you say: then this buyer turns out to sacrifice a burnt offering lacking a limb, since this limb is not his — this is asked in the first chapter of Temura (11b), and answered: for example, where he said, “It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering in its life.”
tosafot:a2.1: It is sold for the needs of a burnt offering: And if you say: does this buyer then sacrifice a burnt offering lacking a limb, since this limb is not his? This is asked in the first chapter of Temura (11b), and it answers: for example, where he said, “It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering in its life,” that is, [an animal] as it can live, even though its leg was cut off from the knee joint down. And the reason it does not answer: for example, where he said, “The leg of this one is a burnt offering, to discharge the burnt offering of so-and-so,” like the one who says in the first chapter of Ḥullin (23b), “It is incumbent upon me to bring bread to discharge the thanks offering of so-and-so” — one may say that it gave that answer only to the wording of an Amora’s statement, but the wording of the baraita does not imply this.
gershom:a1.1: Might it go out: the rest of the animal, to non-sacred status.
gershom:a2.1: It shall be as it is: it shall remain in its sanctity.
gershom:a3.1: Except for the payment for that limb of it: which he consecrated, that its payment shall be sacred.
rashi:a4.1: And even according to the one who says, etc.: so we established at the end of the first chapter of Temura (11b), that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree only about an item on which life does not depend, such as from the knee joint down.
rashi:a5.1: This is our reading: “It is not difficult”; we do not read “Rather.”
rashi:a5.2: This one is with inherent sanctity: the baraita that teaches that the sanctity spreads through all of it is, for example, where he consecrated it with inherent sanctity, saying, “The head of this animal I will sacrifice as a burnt offering.” And the baraita above, that the consecrated property has only the head of the cow, for the altar, is where he consecrated it for its value, saying, “The head of this animal is upon me for the value of a burnt offering,” similar to a slave and a donkey, to which inherent sanctity for sacrifice does not apply.
gershom:a4.1: This is with inherent sanctity, this with sanctity of value: if he consecrated the head of the animal with sanctity of value for the altar, that it be sold and with its money an offering be bought for the altar, certainly [the Temple] has only its head, since it is possible to sell the head alone. But if he consecrated it with inherent sanctity, [to be sacrificed itself on the altar, and it is impossible to divide the head from the body,] the sanctity spreads through all of it, since it is impossible to slaughter the head as a burnt offering and the body as non-sacred, as one does not slaughter non-sacred animals in the Temple courtyard.
rashi:a6.1: But wasn’t it the Master who said: in the first chapter of Temura (11b): if he consecrated a male, a ram, which is fit for a burnt offering, and consecrated it for the value of a burnt offering, it is sanctified with inherent sanctity, and it itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering; for since sanctity of value comes upon it, inherent sanctity comes upon it, as it is fit in itself. So too here: when he says, “The head of a cow for the value of a burnt offering,” let it be sanctified in itself, since it is fit, and let the sanctity spread through all of it.
tosafot:a6.1: But wasn’t it the Master who said: one who consecrates a male for its value: from here it appears that we read “Rabba” [as the one Abaye is answering], since Abaye would not call Rava, his colleague, “Master.” And although we find that Rav Yosef said to Abaye, his student, “The Master, who is a great man, knows what I am saying,” in Zevaḥim, chapter Kodshei Kodashim (62a) — there it is different, since Abaye had understood what others had not understood.
gershom:a5.1: But wasn’t it the Master who said: Rava, in tractate Temura: if he consecrated a male for its value, saying, “The value of this male is a burnt offering,” it is sanctified with inherent sanctity, and the male itself is sacred, since it is fit for the altar. So too here: since this cow is fit for altar offerings, once he consecrated it with sanctity of value, let it have the sanctity of the altar, and let the sanctity spread through all of it.
rashi:a7.1: This is where he consecrated all of it: for its value, and it is sanctified with inherent sanctity, since there is only one “since” [one step of extension].
rashi:a7.2: This is where he consecrated one limb: as here, where he said, “The head of a cow for the value of a burnt offering.” We do not say: since one limb is sanctified, all of it is sanctified too, and since sanctity of value came upon it, inherent sanctity came upon it — for we do not say two “since”s together.
gershom:a6.1: This is where he consecrated all of it: with sanctity of value, it is sanctified with inherent sanctity.
gershom:a7.1: This is where he consecrated one limb: with sanctity of value, it is not sanctified with inherent sanctity.
rashi:a8.1: [Rashi’s text reads: “About a limb, too, the Master raised a dilemma,” i.e., the one being answered raised it himself.] At the end of the first chapter of Temura (11b).
rashi:a8.2: If he consecrated a limb for its value, what is the halakha: is the whole animal sanctified in itself? Do we say: since one limb is sanctified for its value, it is sanctified in itself, and since one limb is sanctified, all of it is sanctified? Or perhaps we do not say two “since”s? And if [your distinction] is right, let the Master resolve it from this baraita, that it is not, since it teaches, “The consecrated property has only its head,” and we established it as dealing with items consecrated for the altar, where he said “for its value.”
gershom:a8.1: What is the halakha: is it sanctified with sanctity of value or with inherent sanctity? Similar to a donkey, which is not sacrificed on the altar.
rashi:a9.1: With an unblemished one: where one could say that inherent sanctity comes upon it, since it is fit for sacrifice. And the baraita, for which it is obvious that not all of it is sanctified, speaks of a blemished animal, similar to a slave and a donkey, which are not fit in themselves.
tosafot:a10.1: As Rabba raised a dilemma: “The value of my head for the altar,” etc., and it remained “let it stand”: that was before we heard the baraita above, as we conclude.
gershom:a9.1: The value of my head for the altar: you have nothing more blemished, as far as the altar is concerned, than a person.
gershom:a10.1: Before we heard this baraita: about the head of a donkey.
rashi:a11.1: “The value of my head for the altar”: is he assessed by its significance, or is he not assessed by its significance and gives half the value? And you have nothing more blemished, as far as the altar is concerned, than this, since he is a person; and yet he raises a dilemma about it. Why? Let him resolve it from that [baraita], that he is not assessed [by its significance].
tosafot:a11.1: (Rabba raised a dilemma: the value of my head for the altar.) This requires study: why did he not put it as “the valuation of my head for the altar,” as in the dilemma that follows?
gershom:a11.1: Assessed by its significance: that of the limb, and he gives the value of his whole body to the altar.
rashi:a12.1: Do we say we have not found: a vow anywhere that is not assessed by its significance; or perhaps we have not found for the altar, etc.
gershom:a12.1: We have not found: [anything] sanctified in valuations that is not assessed by its significance; or perhaps we have not found a blemished thing, for the altar, that is assessed by its significance, as we answered here: with a blemished animal, similar to a donkey.
rashi:a13.1: Assessed by affordability: with regard to a vow or a gift such as this.
tosafot:a13.1: Rava raised a dilemma: “My valuation is upon me for the altar”: if we read “Rabba” in all of them, one can explain it as an “if you say” [that builds on the dilemma] above.
gershom:a13.1: Assessed by affordability: as we said above.
rashi:a15.1: If he consecrated an ancestral field: for the value of a burnt offering.
rashi:a15.2: What is the halakha: how does he redeem it, if he wants to redeem it? For it is obvious to us that had he consecrated it for Temple maintenance, he would redeem it at an area for sowing a ḥomer of barley for fifty silver shekels, as it is a decree of the verse, even if it is worth a thousand zuz.
rashi:a15.3: An ancestral field that is redeemed: for we have found an ancestral field only for Temple maintenance, since unspecified consecrations are for Temple maintenance. Therefore, when he designates it for the altar, he also redeems it only in this way. Or perhaps we have found the altar only at its value, since we have found verses about the altar only concerning animals, and for those the Torah certainly did not set a fixed sum for their redemption if they became blemished; so here too we say: at its value. Let it stand.
rashi:a16.1: Mishna: Less than one month old is the object of a vow: if another said, “His value is upon me,” since he has some value, however small.
rashi:a16.2: But is not valuated: since the passage speaks only of “from a month old and upward.”
rashi:a17.1: Gemara: He gives his assessment: what he would sell for in the market.
gershom:a14.1: He gives his assessment: his worth.
rashi:a19.1: In accordance with Rabbi Meir: who says a person does not utter his words for naught; and a person knows there is no valuation for a utensil, since “persons” is written [in the passage], so he decided and spoke for the sake of assessment.
rashi:a19.2: It is obvious that it is in accordance with Rabbi Meir: why do I need to say, “In accordance with whom is this?”
gershom:a15.1: One who says, “The valuation of a utensil is upon me”: since there is no valuation for a utensil by Torah law. He gives its assessment: in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who says a person does not utter his words for naught.
rashi:a20.1: There: with one less than a month old, the Rabbis exempt him, because one could say: even if a person does not utter his words for naught, that applies only where he knows his words are void. But this one thought there was a valuation for one less than a month old, as for one a month old, and there is none; so it turns out to be a consecration made in error, and he did not speak of value, that he should give the value. But with a utensil, let him be liable. It teaches us that it is Rabbi Meir’s view and not the Rabbis’, since the Rabbis’ reason is that a person does utter his words for naught, even when he knows that these words of his are void.
tosafot:a21.1: A person knows there is no valuation for one less than a month old: and even if he does not know, in any case his intention follows the language the Sages established. And if you say: how is this different from what is said in the chapter Tamid Nishḥat (Pesaḥim 63a): one who intends to say “teruma” and said “tithe,” or “tithe” and said “teruma,” has said nothing? One may say: he has said nothing by what he utters with his mouth, but what is in his heart stands. Alternatively, one may say: there it is different, since what he said with his mouth he does not want, and in what he said in his heart he erred.
rashi:b1.1: And according to Rabbi Meir, why is it necessary: since Rav spoke according to Rabbi Meir and not according to the Rabbis, why was it necessary to say that he gives its value? It is obvious: there, where one could say he erred and did not speak for the sake of value but thought there was a valuation, Rabbi Meir holds him liable; here, where he certainly knows there is no valuation for a utensil, all the more so.
gershom:a16.1: It is obvious: what he holds about the valuation of one less than a month old, he holds about the valuation of a utensil. And according to Rabbi Meir, why was it needed? This ruling of Rav Giddel: he already taught us once that a person does not utter his words for naught.
gershom:b1.1: One might have thought Rabbi Meir’s reason is that he decreed about the valuation of one less than a month old because of one a month old: for if you exempt him from the valuation of one less than a month old, sometimes he will valuate one a month old and think, “I am exempt here too.” But with the valuation of a utensil, where there is no room for error, say he does not give its value. It teaches us [otherwise].
rashi:b3.1: He gives its assessment: for a person knows that consecration does not take effect on something that is not his, so he decided and spoke for the sake of value.
gershom:b2.1: In accordance with whom? Rabbi Meir: here too we say a person knows that one cannot consecrate an animal that is not his, so he decided and spoke for the sake of value.
rashi:b5.1: Let it be consecrated from now, and I will sacrifice it: when I buy it. He intended to consecrate the animal itself, erring in this, but he did not speak of value. Therefore let him give nothing, since his consecration does not take effect on the animal itself, and he did not intend its value.
rashi:b5.2: It teaches us: that we do not say he erred; rather, he certainly knows that his consecration does not take effect on the animal itself, and he intended its value.
gershom:b3.1: Let it be consecrated from now: even though it is not mine, when I buy it I will sacrifice it. He does not consecrate it for its value but has in mind to sacrifice it, and it is sanctified neither for sacrifice nor for value. It teaches us that it is sanctified for value.
rashi:b6.1: And that is where he said “upon me”: [he said,] “The value of this animal of my fellow is upon me, to sacrifice”; he gives its value, since he did not speak of the animal itself but took its value upon himself.
rashi:b6.2: But if he said “this”: and did not say “upon me,” but said, “This animal is a burnt offering,” he has said nothing.
gershom:b4.1: And that is where he said “upon me”: when he said of his fellow’s animal, “This animal is upon me as consecrated property,” he gives its value. But if he said, “This animal is consecrated property,” he is exempt from everything, since a person cannot consecrate what is not his.
rashi:b7.1: Mishna: A gentile is valuated: if a Jew said, “His valuation is upon me,” he gives the valuation according to the gentile’s years.
rashi:b7.2: But does not valuate: but if the gentile said, “My valuation is upon me” or “The valuation of others is upon me,” he has said nothing.
rashi:b7.3: Rabbi Yehuda says: He valuates: if he said of a Jew, “His valuation is upon me.”
rashi:b7.4: But is not valuated: for if he said, “My valuation is upon me,” he has no valuation; or if a Jew said, “The valuation of this gentile is upon me,” he has said nothing.
tosafot:b9.1: One might have thought they are not valuated; the verse states “a man”: And although “a man” is written of the one who valuates, “a man” is written twice; if it is not needed for the one who valuates, apply it to the one who is valuated. And if you say: but in the first chapter of Temura (3a) we exclude gentiles from substitution by this very “a man”? One may say that in the chapter Beit Shammai in tractate Zevaḥim (45a) there is another exposition excluding gentiles from substitution, and it relies on that one: we derive it from the animal tithe, an obligatory offering with no fixed time, which Jews bring and gentiles do not.
gershom:b5.1: Since one verse, etc.: that is, “a man” includes gentiles and “the children of Israel” excludes them; for what reason, etc.
rashi:b12.1: Gemara: “A man”: implies anyone at all.
gershom:b6.1: Because the verse included: more among those who valuate than among those who are valuated, since a tumtum and a hermaphrodite valuate but are not valuated.
gershom:b7.1: And if you say: set the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor against the tumtum and the hermaphrodite, and those who are valuated come out more than those who valuate — this is not difficult: [all three,] the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor, count as one, since they lack understanding. Moreover, [the verse] included gentiles more [among those who valuate] than among those who are valuated, since the tumtum and the hermaphrodite vow, are the object of vows, and valuate, and a gentile [too] vows and is the object of vows; [therefore it is preferable,] to the exclusion of the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor, who are not the object of vows. [So the text reads; the mishna on 2a says they are the object of vows but do not vow.]
rashi:b15.1: Rabbi Meir’s halakha is reasonable: that gentiles do not valuate.
rashi:b15.2: And his reason is not reasonable: since he derives his reason from a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor, and one can refute this: there, it is because they are not competent, since they also do not vow and do not consecrate. But a gentile, who does vow and consecrate — for Rabbi Meir concedes that he vows and is the object of vows — say that he also valuates, were it not for this verse, “You have nothing to do with us,” written in the book of Ezra, where the gentiles were volunteering and wanted to help them build the Second Temple, and Neḥemya son of Ḥakhalya said to them: “You have nothing to do with us to build; rather, we alone.” [In Ezra 4:3 the reply is given by Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the heads of the fathers’ houses.]
tosafot:b15.1: A deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor are different, since they are not competent: and Rabbi Meir, who derives from them, holds that they are somewhat alike, since they are valuated even though they do not valuate; so too he can say of gentiles.
gershom:b8.1: Rabbi Meir’s halakha is reasonable: [Rabbi Meir’s ruling] appears correct; [his reason does not appear correct.]
gershom:b9.1: [Rabbi Meir’s halakha is reasonable: that he does not valuate, since] it is written, “You have nothing to do with us to build a house”: that is, those men, Sanballat and Toviya, who were gentiles — they did not let them build and consecrate for the needs of Temple maintenance.
gershom:b10.1: Evidently gentiles do not valuate, since valuations too are for Temple maintenance. But they are valuated, since a Jew can valuate them, as it is a Jew’s money.
gershom:b11.1: [His reason is not reasonable, since he brings it from a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor:] for he says that a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor are valuated but do not valuate. Perhaps they do not valuate because they are not competent; but a gentile, who is competent, one could say does valuate.
rashi:b16.1: Rabbi Yehuda’s reason is reasonable: for it is certainly more reasonable to apply the exclusion the verse makes to those who are valuated, and the inclusion to those who valuate, since the tumtum and the hermaphrodite, who are competent like gentiles, valuate but are not valuated, for the verse excluded them, as it is written, “the male” (Leviticus 27:3): from the extra letter heh we expound, a definite male, and not a tumtum or a hermaphrodite.
rashi:b16.2: And his halakha is not reasonable: for he certainly does not valuate, since valuations are for Temple maintenance, and the verse writes, “You have nothing to do with us to build.”
gershom:b12.1: Since he brings it from a tumtum and a hermaphrodite: although they are competent, the Merciful One excluded them from being valuated, because [the verse requires] a definite male and a definite female. But as for valuating, since they are competent, [they valuate]; gentiles too, since they are competent, valuate, but are not valuated, since the Merciful One excluded them too, by “the children of Israel.”
gershom:b13.1: His halakha is not reasonable: since it is written, “You have nothing to do with us.”
rashi:b17.1: Avimi said: that Rabbi Yehuda said they valuate is not because it goes to Temple maintenance, since it is written, “You have nothing to do with us”; rather, it is sacred and interred, as it is forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b14.1: What does he do with it: implying that their valuation does not enter Temple maintenance. Rabbi Yehuda holds that they certainly valuate; Rav Ḥisda said: and their valuation is interred, so that it does not fall to Temple maintenance, since it is written, “You have nothing to do with us.”
rashi:b18.1: If that is so: since it goes to destruction, let one not be liable for misuse of it: one who benefits from it should not be liable to bring a misuse offering, for we learned: sin offerings left to die — the sin offerings listed in Temura: the offspring of a sin offering, the substitute of a sin offering, etc.
tosafot:b18.1: If that is so, let one not be liable for misuse of it: according to Rabbi Yehuda. Why then is it taught, “But with consecrations for Temple maintenance one is liable for misuse”? To whom will you attribute it? It certainly cannot be established according to Rabbi Meir, since he takes his halakha from “You have nothing to do with us,” which shows that gentiles do not consecrate for Temple maintenance at all; and, at least [as Avimi explains him], it does not fit Rabbi Yehuda. Nor can one explain that according to the conclusion, that it is due to the weakening of hands, it fits Rabbi Meir well, for that is not so: Rabbi Meir does not hold this reason, for if so, from where would he derive the halakha that gentiles do not valuate, from the verse “You have nothing to do with us”? And it requires study: since according to Rabbi Meir gentiles do not donate to Temple maintenance, how did we learn [in the mishna], “Both agree that they vow”? According to Rabbi Meir, gentiles do not vow for Temple maintenance! And it is forced to explain that “they vow” refers to the altar, since the mishna apparently parallels valuations, which are for Temple maintenance. And perhaps it is good to explain that with this conclusion Rava retracted what he said at first, that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir because of the verse “You have nothing to do with us.”
gershom:b15.1: If that is so: since their valuation is interred, one should not be liable for misuse of it.
rashi:b18.2: And money that goes to the Dead Sea: which is like a sin offering whose owner died, which is left to die; and if a person benefited from them he is not liable to bring an offering, since “from the sacred things of the Lord” (Leviticus 5:15) does not apply to it, as they go to destruction.
gershom:b16.1: One may not derive benefit, and there is no liability for misuse: if one benefited from them.
rashi:b19.1: Whereas regarding the consecrations of gentiles it is taught: in Sheḥitat Kodashim [Zevaḥim], in the chapter Beit Shammai (Zevaḥim 45b).
rashi:b19.2: In what case is this said: that misuse does not apply to the consecrations of gentiles — that is with items consecrated for the altar, since we derive misuse from teruma through “sin” and “sin” [a verbal analogy]: just as with teruma, death [at the hand of Heaven] applies only to the teruma of Jews, as it is written explicitly, “And they shall not profane the sacred things of the children of Israel” (Leviticus 22:15), so too misuse applies only to the consecrations of Jews.
rashi:b19.3: But consecrations: of gentiles for Temple maintenance are subject to misuse. And it explains the reason there: when misuse is derived from teruma through “sin” and “sin,” it is like teruma, which has inherent sanctity; but sanctity of value we do not derive from it. I found this reason stated in Zevaḥim, and it is the main one, since it is taught there explicitly. And from my teacher I heard: items gentiles consecrated for the altar are not subject to misuse because we have found a distinction between gentiles’ altar consecrations and Jews’ altar consecrations, in that one is not liable for them for piggul, notar or impurity, as we say in the first passage of Temura (2b); but with gentiles’ consecrations for Temple maintenance we have found no distinction, and therefore they are subject to misuse. This I heard, but the first is the main one. In any case it teaches that they are subject to misuse; evidently it is not interred, since misuse applies to it.
gershom:b17.1: Why is it taught: in tractate Me’ila, about the consecrations of gentiles: In what case is this said? With altar consecrations, which are not subject to misuse; but with consecrations for Temple maintenance one is liable for misuse. And these too, if they are interred, are like money that goes to the Dead Sea, and one should not be liable for misuse of them.
rashi:b20.1: Rather, Rava said: it certainly goes to Temple maintenance; and in Ezra’s days, this was the reason they sent them, “You have nothing to do with us.”
rashi:b20.2: Due to weakening of the hands: because they did not intend good, but wanted [the Jews] to rely on them as well and listen to their advice, and they would delay the building until they turned Cyrus’s heart against building it.
gershom:b18.1: Rather, Rava said: Rabbi Yehuda actually holds that their valuation is sacred like other consecrated property and subject to misuse. And what is the reason for “You have nothing to do with us to build”? Due to the weakening of hands: lest, if they donate and want to build with them, they make them stop, since their heart was not for the sake of Heaven, as it is written, “Then the people of the land [weakened the hands of the people of Judah],” etc.
